newsitem.title: UK: Profits may dull incentives to scrap old tankers.
newsitem.headline: Profits may dull incentives to scrap old tankers.

text.p: Tanker owners may come under growing pressure this year to scrap ageing vessels but some analysts say there is little incentive to do so as long as they remain profitable.

"There is an increased awareness of vessel quality that is governing the market, with less opportunity for poorly maintained tonnage," said Mark Jenkins, research director at brokers Simpson, Spence & Young (SS&Y).
He said there were signs of greater willingness in some countries to combat leaking vessels, especially in the Middle East Gulf.
Countries such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were indicating that they may ban vessels without segregated ballasts, which would "at a stroke preclude 1970s-built ships," he said.
"There is a groundswell of opinion that maybe one or two countries will take the plunge in 1997," Jenkins said.
Segregated ballasts separate clean and dirty ballast water so that the former can be safely discharged at sea while the latter is emptied into tanks on land.
Although they believe scrappings may increase this year, SS&Y expect removals from the tanker fleet to be lower in 1996 than in 1995 when final numbers are in.

SS&Y put total tanker deletions to November 30, 1996 at 9.08 million deadweight tonnes (dwt), against 10.75 million dwt in the whole of 1995, with the sharpest fall in very large crude carriers (VLCCs) above 200,000 dwt.
But other analysts were not convinced increased environmental awareness is likely to result in increased scrappings in 1997.
"In essence the level of scrappings is primarily driven by freight rates," said Ian Dixon of Drewry Shipping Consultants.
He said freight rates were likely to remain firm this year.
"Owners are not going to scrap vessels when they can continue to make a profit unless the ship's falling to pieces.
"Any (rise in) scrapping will be on the back of very exceptional scrapping prices and we're not going to see that in the next few years."
In a recent World Tanker Fleet Review, Jacobs & Partners said there were plenty of charterers willing to hire old ships.

"As long as older VLCCs remain acceptable to charterers at rates similar to those awarded to modern ships, making them profitable in spite of higher bunker consumption and maintenance costs, there is little incentive to scrap," they said.
But despite expectations of low scrappings, a Jacobs analyst said the world VLCC fleet will still drop in dwt terms since there were few new orders which would feed into 1997 deliveries.
But analysts sees a steady growth in new vessels smaller than VLCCs hitting the market.
Analysts at Drewry said the market for newbuildings may be given a lift by signs of greater flexibility over payment terms by South Korean shipyards, the world's leading tanker builder.

Analysts said steady growth in non-VLCC tonnage was coming onto the market to cope with a 1.9 million barrels per day (bpd) rise in world oil demand this year, forecast by the International Energy Agency.
They said demand for ships other than VLCCs was being stoked by fast rising output from non-OPEC countries, some of which have ports that cannot handle VLCCs.
